The Mo substrate supplies electrons through two thin MgO layers to the two-dimensional Au20\mathrm{Au}_{20}Au20​ interface. These electrons enter the 2π∗2\pi^*2π∗ antibonding states of adsorbed oxygen and lengthen O–O. CO on a neighboring MgO site can then react with it over a low barrier. The gold-cluster interface anchors and activates oxygen, while the MgO site allows CO to approach from a suitable direction. Zhang, Yoon & Landman (2007)

Mo supplies electrons through thin MgO to the gold-cluster interface. As the C–O distance decreases, the system crosses a maximum of approximately 0.15 eV0.15\,\mathrm{eV}0.15eV and forms carbon dioxide.

This LH path starts from configuration aaa, in which CO and oxygen are coadsorbed. The scan coordinate is the distance from the C atom in CO to the nearest O atom in the oxygen molecule:

q=d(C,O(2)).q=d(\mathrm C,\mathrm O^{(2)}). q=d(C,O(2)).

The C–O distance starts at 2.85 A˚2.85\,\text{\AA}2.85A˚ in the initial state. In configuration bbb near the maximum, it has shortened to 1.60 A˚1.60\,\text{\AA}1.60A˚, while O–O has lengthened from 1.521.521.52 to 1.55 A˚1.55\,\text{\AA}1.55A˚. After the new C–O bond forms, CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ leaves the surface. Relative to the coadsorbed initial state, the barrier along this path is approximately:

E‡=E(b)−E(a)≃0.15 eV.E^\ddagger=E(b)-E(a)\simeq0.15\,\mathrm{eV}. E‡=E(b)−E(a)≃0.15eV.

If the horizontal axis is the C–O distance itself, the reaction proceeds toward decreasing distance. The peak height measures the barrier, while the subsequent energy decrease represents the energy released in product formation.

The adsorption site of CO changes the path. CO adsorbed at the Au edge gives a barrier of approximately 1.0 eV1.0\,\mathrm{eV}1.0eV; an ER path in which gas-phase CO directly attacks adsorbed oxygen has a barrier of approximately 0.2 eV0.2\,\mathrm{eV}0.2eV. The low barrier combines electronic and geometric effects: oxygen first gains antibonding electrons, and CO then approaches the activated oxygen from a neighboring MgO site. Zhang, Yoon & Landman (2007), Supporting Information


Finding a reaction path

From one reaction coordinate to a chain of configurations

A single bond length describes some reactions clearly, but molecular rotation, concerted changes in several bonds, or surface reconstruction often require more coordinates. NEB (nudged elastic band) starts from known initial and final states and directly optimizes a chain of complete configurations, allowing the whole chain to bend toward a low-energy channel.

The endpoints lie in two energy minima. The initial path must adjust in configuration space to pass through the low-energy channel connecting them.

A configuration of NNN atoms is written as:

R=(x1,y1,z1,…,xN,yN,zN),E=E(R).\mathbf R=(x_1,y_1,z_1,\ldots,x_N,y_N,z_N), \qquad E=E(\mathbf R). R=(x1​,y1​,z1​,…,xN​,yN​,zN​),E=E(R).

An image consists of the complete atomic coordinates and the corresponding potential energy and forces. A two-dimensional contour plot is only a schematic of the high-dimensional potential energy surface (PES): each point represents the entire atomic system. Fixing some substrate atoms reduces the number of degrees of freedom that can be optimized.

Each iteration first solves the electronic problem at the corresponding geometry. Magnetic systems also require tracking the electronic spin state and using consistent spin treatment across all images. The nuclear path is optimized on the selected electronic potential energy surface; transitions between different spin surfaces require a nonadiabatic treatment.

Discretize the path as:

R0,R1,…,RM−1,RM.\mathbf R_0,\mathbf R_1,\ldots,\mathbf R_{M-1},\mathbf R_M. R0​,R1​,…,RM−1​,RM​.

There are M+1M+1M+1 images. R0\mathbf R_0R0​ and RM\mathbf R_MRM​ are the optimized IS and FS and are usually fixed, while the intermediate images are optimized together. The distances between neighboring configurations are:

di+=∣Ri+1−Ri∣,di−=∣Ri−Ri−1∣.d_i^+=|\mathbf R_{i+1}-\mathbf R_i|, \qquad d_i^-=|\mathbf R_i-\mathbf R_{i-1}|. di+​=∣Ri+1​−Ri​∣,di−​=∣Ri​−Ri−1​∣.

With a Cartesian metric, square and sum all displacement components of corresponding atoms, then take the square root. All images must therefore share consistent atom counts, element ordering, atom correspondence, and cell descriptions.

More images resolve curved paths, intermediate minima, and variations near the maximum, at the cost of more electronic-structure calculations. Usually, first establish a clear channel, then increase sampling where the path changes rapidly. The energies can be plotted against cumulative configuration-space distance after optimization; this measures reaction progress, not elapsed time.

Why NEB projects the forces

If each intermediate configuration is minimized independently, the images fall into energy minima and leave the barrier region unsampled. Ordinary connecting springs can instead straighten a curved path to shorten the band, causing corner cutting. NEB separates the two tasks: the physical force moves the path perpendicular to its tangent toward the valley, while the spring force distributes images along the path.

Tangential and perpendicular components of the physical force

The physical force on image iii is:

Fiphys=−∇E(Ri).\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{phys}}=-\nabla E(\mathbf R_i). Fiphys​=−∇E(Ri​).

Let τi\boldsymbol\tau_iτi​ be a unit tangent estimated from neighboring configurations, satisfying τi⋅τi=1\boldsymbol\tau_i\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_i=1τi​⋅τi​=1. The projection of the physical force along the path is:

Fi,∥phys=(Fiphys⋅τi)τi.\mathbf F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{phys}} =(\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_i)\boldsymbol\tau_i. Fi,∥phys​=(Fiphys​⋅τi​)τi​.

The dot product gives the scalar tangential component. Multiplying by the unit tangent gives its vector projection. Subtracting this projection leaves the perpendicular component:

Fi,⊥phys=Fiphys−(Fiphys⋅τi)τi.\mathbf F_{i,\perp}^{\mathrm{phys}} =\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{phys}} -(\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_i)\boldsymbol\tau_i. Fi,⊥phys​=Fiphys​−(Fiphys​⋅τi​)τi​.

It satisfies Fi,⊥phys⋅τi=0\mathbf F_{i,\perp}^{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_i=0Fi,⊥phys​⋅τi​=0. Normalize the tangent before applying these formulas directly.

The physical tangential force would push images toward the energy minima, so ordinary NEB removes it. The retained perpendicular force lets the path move down the valley walls toward the MEP. A converged MEP satisfies:

F⊥phys=0.\mathbf F_\perp^{\mathrm{phys}}=\mathbf 0. F⊥phys​=0.

A tangential downhill force can still exist along the MEP. The complete physical force vanishes only at the TS or another stationary point.

Retaining only the tangential spring force

With a uniform spring constant kkk, the tangential spring force is:

Fi,∥spring=k(di+−di−)τi.\mathbf F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{spring}} =k(d_i^+-d_i^-)\boldsymbol\tau_i. Fi,∥spring​=k(di+​−di−​)τi​.

When the forward spacing is larger, the spring pulls the image along +τi+\boldsymbol\tau_i+τi​. Tangential balance makes the forward and backward spacings equal. The perpendicular spring component is removed so that it does not straighten a curved channel.

The effective force used for optimization is therefore:

FiNEB=Fi,⊥phys+Fi,∥spring.\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{NEB}} =\mathbf F_{i,\perp}^{\mathrm{phys}} +\mathbf F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{spring}}. FiNEB​=Fi,⊥phys​+Fi,∥spring​.

kkk can be expressed in eV A˚−2\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2}eVA˚−2. Multiplying by a configuration-space distance gives force units of eV A˚−1\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-1}eVA˚−1.

For example, take τ=(1,0)\boldsymbol\tau=(1,0)τ=(1,0) and Fphys=(2,−3) eV A˚−1\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}}=(2,-3)\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-1}Fphys=(2,−3)eVA˚−1, forward and backward spacings of 222 and 1 A˚1\,\text{\AA}1A˚, and k=1.5 eV A˚−2k=1.5\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2}k=1.5eVA˚−2. The perpendicular physical force is (0,−3)(0,-3)(0,−3) and the spring force is (1.5,0)(1.5,0)(1.5,0), giving:

FNEB=(1.5,−3) eV A˚−1.\mathbf F^{\mathrm{NEB}}=(1.5,-3)\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-1}. FNEB=(1.5,−3)eVA˚−1.

FiNEB=0\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{NEB}}=0FiNEB​=0 means that the perpendicular physical force vanishes and the tangential spring forces balance. The removed physical tangential force can remain nonzero, so an ordinary converged image can lie on a slope of the MEP.

Variable spring constants: denser sampling at high energy

Accurate peak energies require denser sampling near the saddle point. Increasing the spring constants in high-energy regions concentrates the available images in these segments.

Let kik_iki​ connect images i−1i-1i−1 and iii, and define:

Eref=max⁡(EIS,EFS),E~i=max⁡(Ei−1,Ei),E_{\mathrm{ref}}=\max(E_{\mathrm{IS}},E_{\mathrm{FS}}), \qquad \widetilde E_i=\max(E_{i-1},E_i), Eref​=max(EIS​,EFS​),Ei​=max(Ei−1​,Ei​),

Δk=kmax⁡−kmin⁡.\Delta k=k_{\max}-k_{\min}. Δk=kmax​−kmin​.

Emax⁡E_{\max}Emax​ is the highest physical energy on the current band. Assign each segment's spring constant using the higher energy of its two endpoints:

ki={kmax⁡−Δk Emax⁡−E~iEmax⁡−Eref,E~i>Eref,kmin⁡,E~i≤Eref.k_i= \begin{cases} k_{\max}-\Delta k\,\dfrac{E_{\max}-\widetilde E_i}{E_{\max}-E_{\mathrm{ref}}}, &\widetilde E_i>E_{\mathrm{ref}},\\[6pt] k_{\min},&\widetilde E_i\leq E_{\mathrm{ref}}. \end{cases} ki​=⎩⎪⎪⎨⎪⎪⎧​kmax​−ΔkEmax​−Eref​Emax​−Ei​​,kmin​,​Ei​>Eref​,Ei​≤Eref​.​

When E~i=Emax⁡\widetilde E_i=E_{\max}Ei​=Emax​, the segment uses the stiffest spring, kmax⁡k_{\max}kmax​. As its energy decreases to ErefE_{\mathrm{ref}}Eref​, the constant returns continuously to kmin⁡k_{\min}kmin​. If Emax⁡=ErefE_{\max}=E_{\mathrm{ref}}Emax​=Eref​, use constant springs to avoid a zero denominator.

When the forward and backward spring constants differ, the tangential force is:

Fi,∥spring=(ki+1di+−kidi−)τi.\mathbf F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{spring}} =(k_{i+1}d_i^+-k_i d_i^-)\boldsymbol\tau_i. Fi,∥spring​=(ki+1​di+​−ki​di−​)τi​.

Tangential equilibrium requires equal tensions on the two sides:

ki+1di+≈kidi−.k_{i+1}d_i^+\approx k_i d_i^-. ki+1​di+​≈ki​di−​.

At the same tension, a larger kkk gives a smaller spacing, so more images gather in high-energy regions. These springs control numerical sampling; they leave the physical potential energy unchanged.

For example, with Eref=0E_{\mathrm{ref}}=0Eref​=0, Emax⁡=0.8 eVE_{\max}=0.8\,\mathrm{eV}Emax​=0.8eV, kmin⁡=1k_{\min}=1kmin​=1, and kmax⁡=5 eV A˚−2k_{\max}=5\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2}kmax​=5eVA˚−2, a segment at E~i=0.6 eV\widetilde E_i=0.6\,\mathrm{eV}Ei​=0.6eV has:

ki=5−40.8−0.60.8=4 eV A˚−2.k_i=5-4\frac{0.8-0.6}{0.8} =4\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2}. ki​=5−40.80.8−0.6​=4eVA˚−2.

Climbing Image NEB: moving directly toward a saddle point

The highest sampled image in ordinary NEB may lie on one side of the maximum. CI-NEB selects an image and drives it uphill along the path and downhill perpendicular to the path, directly toward the saddle point.

The physical force decomposes as F⊥+F∥\mathbf F_\perp+\mathbf F_\parallelF⊥​+F∥​. Retaining the perpendicular component and reversing the tangential component gives the target force F⊥−F∥\mathbf F_\perp-\mathbf F_\parallelF⊥​−F∥​. This is equivalent to subtracting twice the tangential component from the physical force:

FCI=Fphys−2(Fphys⋅τ)τ.\mathbf F^{\mathrm{CI}} =\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}} -2(\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau)\boldsymbol\tau. FCI=Fphys−2(Fphys⋅τ)τ.

Substituting Fphys=−∇E\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}}=-\nabla EFphys=−∇E gives:

FCI=−∇E+2(∇E⋅τ)τ.\mathbf F^{\mathrm{CI}} =-\nabla E+2(\nabla E\cdot\boldsymbol\tau)\boldsymbol\tau. FCI=−∇E+2(∇E⋅τ)τ.

First obtain a reasonable channel with ordinary NEB. Then select the highest-energy intermediate image as the climbing image and remove its spring force. It can then reach the maximum without being constrained by equal spacing. The other images continue to use ordinary NEB forces and provide the path shape and local tangent.

Using the same example with τ=(1,0)\boldsymbol\tau=(1,0)τ=(1,0) and Fphys=(2,−3)\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}}=(2,-3)Fphys=(2,−3):

FCI=(2,−3)−2(2,0)=(−2,−3).\mathbf F^{\mathrm{CI}} =(2,-3)-2(2,0)=(-2,-3). FCI=(2,−3)−2(2,0)=(−2,−3).

The tangential component reverses sign, the perpendicular component stays unchanged, and no spring force is added.

The tangential and perpendicular directions are orthogonal, so FCI=0\mathbf F^{\mathrm{CI}}=0FCI=0 requires both components of the physical force to vanish, giving a physical stationary point. Check for one reaction-related negative-curvature mode and verify the initial and final states reached by descending in both directions along that mode to identify the intended TS.

Barrier accuracy has two aspects: whether the path has found the intended channel, and whether sampling near the maximum is sufficient. Different initial guesses for competing mechanisms address the first; more images and CI refinement address the second.

Constructing and optimizing the initial path

The simplest initial path is generated by linear interpolation:

Ri(0)=(1−iM)RIS+iMRFS,i=0,…,M.\mathbf R_i^{(0)} =\left(1-\frac{i}{M}\right)\mathbf R_{\mathrm{IS}} +\frac{i}{M}\mathbf R_{\mathrm{FS}}, \qquad i=0,\ldots,M. Ri(0)​=(1−Mi​)RIS​+Mi​RFS​,i=0,…,M.

Every coordinate is interpolated with weight i/Mi/Mi/M, so the initial images are equally spaced in Cartesian configuration space. Their energy spacing depends on the potential energy surface. The endpoints should use consistent cells, atom numbering, constraints, electronic states, and computational accuracy.

For an atom moving from (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) to (2,1) A˚(2,1)\,\text{\AA}(2,1)A˚ with five images in total, M=4M=4M=4. The three internal initial guesses are (0.5,0.25)(0.5,0.25)(0.5,0.25), (1,0.5)(1,0.5)(1,0.5), and (1.5,0.75) A˚(1.5,0.75)\,\text{\AA}(1.5,0.75)A˚. A many-atom system interpolates all coordinates simultaneously.

Inspect each interpolated geometry. Linear interpolation can make two exchanging atoms coincide, or compress internal bonds when a molecule rotates substantially. Add physically reasonable intermediate configurations or interpolate in segments when needed. With periodic boundaries, first unwrap coordinates onto a continuous branch consistent with the intended hop, then generate the path.

The NEB optimization proceeds as follows:

  1. Calculate the electronic energy and physical atomic forces for each image.
  2. Estimate and normalize the tangent from neighboring configurations.
  3. Combine the perpendicular physical force with the tangential spring force and update the intermediate configurations.
  4. Once the path is stable, activate the climbing image and refine the saddle point.
  5. Check electronic self-consistency, converged forces, structural continuity, and sampling near the maximum. Extract the barrier from the energy difference between the relevant IS and TS.

Surface diffusion as a path-search problem

Chemical reactions connect structures with different bonding, while surface diffusion connects different adsorption positions. Both are transitions between minima on a potential energy surface, so both can be studied with NEB.

Diffusion may involve molecular rotation, coordination changes, and surface relaxation. The energy difference from the starting adsorption site to the CI-NEB saddle point is the barrier for that hop. A simple hopping model is:

Γ=νexp⁡ ⁣(−EdiffkBT).\Gamma=\nu\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{\mathrm{diff}}}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right). Γ=νexp(−kB​TEdiff​​).

Γ\GammaΓ is the hopping rate, ν\nuν the attempt frequency, and EdiffE_{\mathrm{diff}}Ediff​ the diffusion barrier. If the endpoints have different energies, the reverse barrier through the same saddle satisfies:

Earev=Eafwd−ΔE.E_a^{\mathrm{rev}}=E_a^{\mathrm{fwd}}-\Delta E. Earev​=Eafwd​−ΔE.

A deeper adsorption site requires more energy to escape. Equal endpoint energies imply equal forward and reverse barriers, but a high maximum can still lie between them. Obtaining a macroscopic diffusion coefficient from a single-hop rate also requires the hop distance, spatial dimension, accessible neighbors, and correlations between hops.

Graphene/Ru: from substrate defects to two-step CO oxidation

Local defects in the Ru surface weaken bonding between Ru and the carbon atoms above them, making those carbon atoms more able to donate electrons to adsorbed oxygen. Occupation of oxygen antibonding states lengthens O–O. Oxygen then reacts with gas-phase CO over relatively low barriers to form carbon dioxide. Guo, Yam & Zhang (2018)

Two substrate defects are considered: IA denotes a substitutional impurity atom replacing a surface Ru atom, and V denotes a single vacancy in the surface Ru layer. The active region lies in the graphene directly above the defect, where oxygen adsorbs on carbon atoms.

IA and V denote two substrate-defect types. The two energy profiles below describe consecutive oxidation steps in the same Au-substitution model, with barriers of 0.540.540.54 and 0.48 eV0.48\,\mathrm{eV}0.48eV.

The specific two-step reaction uses the same Au-substituted Ru(0001) model, with graphene in the fcc-top registry. Au weakens nearby C–Ru bonding; upon oxygen adsorption, electrons enter the oxygen 2π∗2\pi^*2π∗ antibonding states. Oxygen gains approximately 0.99∣e∣0.99|e|0.99∣e∣, O–O lengthens from 1.231.231.23 to 1.48 A˚1.48\,\text{\AA}1.48A˚, and the adsorption energy is −0.43 eV-0.43\,\mathrm{eV}−0.43eV.

Gas-phase CO reacts with adsorbed oxygen through an Eley–Rideal (ER) mechanism. Near the first TS, O–O stretches while a new C–O bond forms. The first CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ molecule is released, leaving one adsorbed oxygen atom:

COgas+O2,ads⟶CO2+Oads,Ea,1=0.54 eV.\mathrm{CO}_{\mathrm{gas}}+\mathrm O_{2,\mathrm{ads}} \longrightarrow\mathrm{CO}_2+\mathrm O_{\mathrm{ads}}, \qquad E_{a,1}=0.54\,\mathrm{eV}. COgas​+O2,ads​⟶CO2​+Oads​,Ea,1​=0.54eV.

A second CO removes the remaining oxygen, forming another carbon dioxide molecule:

COgas+Oads⟶CO2,Ea,2=0.48 eV.\mathrm{CO}_{\mathrm{gas}}+\mathrm O_{\mathrm{ads}} \longrightarrow\mathrm{CO}_2, \qquad E_{a,2}=0.48\,\mathrm{eV}. COgas​+Oads​⟶CO2​,Ea,2​=0.48eV.

These barriers belong to consecutive steps in the same Au system, each measured from its own initial state to its CI-NEB saddle point. After the second step, the graphene site can accept another oxygen molecule and begin the next cycle. Guo, Yam & Zhang (2018)

The rate constant of each step can be understood using a thermally activated form:

ki≃Aiexp⁡ ⁣(−Ea,ikBT).k_i\simeq A_i\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{a,i}}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right). ki​≃Ai​exp(−kB​TEa,i​​).

The first step requires adsorbed oxygen molecules, whereas the second requires the remaining oxygen atoms. Their coverages depend on adsorption and the preceding reactions. Identifying the rate-determining step therefore requires both the local rate constants and these surface populations. Electron transfer explains oxygen activation, CI-NEB describes barrier crossing, and the complete cycle explains sustained site turnover.

A neutral surface reaction can often be followed on one potential energy surface at fixed composition. At an electrode, two consecutive intermediates can differ by a proton drawn from the solution and an electron drawn from the metal. The free energy of that step includes the cost of supplying both. The electrode potential then matters even before looking for a saddle point.

Electrode potential and reaction free energy

A molecule arriving at a metal electrode can draw an electron from the metal and a proton from the solution. Those two particles have different sources. A potentiostat controls the energy at which the metal supplies electrons, while the solution sets the proton activity. This gives an experimentalist two ways to change the free energy of a hydrogenation step without changing the catalyst.

Where the current flows

In the late eighteenth century, Luigi Galvani observed that a frog's leg could twitch when metal contacts completed a circuit through its nerve and muscle. Modern electrochemical cells also join electronic and ionic conductors. Electrons travel through the metal electrodes and the external circuit. In the electrolyte, moving ions carry charge. If the electrodes sit in separate solutions, a salt bridge provides the ionic connection and prevents charge from building up in either compartment. Galvani's account

Oxidation releases electrons at the anode and reduction consumes them at the cathode. During discharge, a lithium-ion battery sends electrons through an external load while lithium ions move through the electrolyte toward the positive electrode. Charging reverses both flows and stores electrical work as chemical free energy. An electrolyser uses an external power supply in the same way to drive a chosen reaction.

The working electrode is the surface whose reaction we want to study. The counter electrode completes the circuit through a second reaction. In a three-electrode measurement, a reference electrode senses the working-electrode potential while drawing negligible current. A voltage quoted for one electrode, such as −0.20 V-0.20\,\mathrm{V}−0.20V versus a hydrogen reference, differs from the voltage applied across the whole cell. The latter includes the counter-electrode potential and voltage losses in the electrolyte.

At the working surface, excess electronic charge attracts counterions and reorients nearby solvent molecules. The resulting electric double layer can sustain a large electric field over a molecular distance. Potential therefore affects a reaction in two ways. It changes the electron energy available for transfer, and it can change how a polar molecule binds and orients in that field. A reaction that keeps running also carries a Faradaic current as electrons cross the interface through chemical steps.

The hydrogen reference and the cost of driving a reaction

The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) establishes the zero for aqueous electrode potentials. Platinum in contact with hydrogen at its standard pressure of 1 bar1\,\mathrm{bar}1bar and protons at unit activity equilibrates the reaction 2H++2e−⇌H22\mathrm H^+ + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons \mathrm H_22H++2e−⇌H2​. By convention its standard potential is zero. Raising the potential UUU of another electrode lowers its electron electrochemical potential μ~e\tilde\mu_eμ~​e​ by e ΔUe\,\Delta UeΔU, where e>0e>0e>0 is the elementary charge. A more negative electrode can supply a more energetic electron. IUPAC definition of the SHE

Consider water electrolysis in acid. The oxygen-evolving anode oxidizes water, and the hydrogen-evolving cathode reduces protons.

2H2O⟶O2+4H++4e−,4H++4e−⟶2H2.\begin{aligned} 2\mathrm H_2\mathrm O &\longrightarrow \mathrm O_2+4\mathrm H^++4e^-,\\ 4\mathrm H^++4e^- &\longrightarrow 2\mathrm H_2 . \end{aligned} 2H2​O4H++4e−​⟶O2​+4H++4e−,⟶2H2​.​

The reversible voltage is approximately 1.23 V1.23\,\mathrm V1.23V at 298 K298\,\mathrm K298K under standard conditions. Splitting two water molecules transfers four electrons, so the minimum electrical work per reaction as written is 4e×1.23 V=4.92 eV4e\times1.23\,\mathrm V=4.92\,\mathrm{eV}4e×1.23V=4.92eV. At finite current, the anode usually needs a more positive potential and the cathode a more negative one. For either electrode the signed overpotential is η=U−Ueq\eta=U-U_{\mathrm{eq}}η=U−Ueq​, with UeqU_{\mathrm{eq}}Ueq​ evaluated for the same reaction and activities. For example, an oxygen-evolving anode at 1.50 V1.50\,\mathrm V1.50V versus RHE under standard gas conditions has an anodic overpotential of about 0.27 V0.27\,\mathrm V0.27V. The cell voltage also includes any ohmic drop between the electrodes. IUPAC electrochemical terminology

Nitrogen reduction uses six electrons for every nitrogen molecule:

N2+6H++6e−⟶2NH3.\mathrm N_2+6\mathrm H^++6e^-\longrightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_3 . N2​+6H++6e−⟶2NH3​.

Couple this half-reaction to hydrogen oxidation, 3H2→6H++6e−3\mathrm H_2\rightarrow 6\mathrm H^++6e^-3H2​→6H++6e−, to obtain N2+3H2→2NH3\mathrm N_2+3\mathrm H_2\rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_3N2​+3H2​→2NH3​. For gaseous ammonia at standard conditions the latter reaction has ΔrG∘≃−32.8 kJ mol−1\Delta_{\mathrm r}G^\circ\simeq-32.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}Δr​G∘≃−32.8kJmol−1. The corresponding standard reduction potential is −ΔrG∘/(6F)≃+0.057 V-\Delta_{\mathrm r}G^\circ/(6F)\simeq+0.057\,\mathrm V−Δr​G∘/(6F)≃+0.057V versus SHE, where FFF is the Faraday constant. Specifying gaseous ammonia matters because dissolved ammonia and ammonium have different chemical potentials. Using hydrogen oxidation to define the reference also leaves us free to build a real cell with a different anode, for instance one that evolves oxygen. Westhead et al. (2023)

A favourable overall free energy says little about the first electron or proton transfer. An isolated N2\mathrm N_2N2​ molecule has a strong triple bond and a large gap between its occupied and unoccupied frontier orbitals. A surface can help by binding the molecule, mixing its orbitals with metal states and stabilizing partially hydrogenated species. Linear CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ also has a large frontier-orbital gap. Representative molecular estimates are around 101010 eV for both molecules and depend on how the orbital energies are evaluated. An electrode potential acts on surface-bound intermediates, whose electronic states and bonding differ from those of the isolated molecule. In CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ reduction, CO and formic acid each require two electrons per carbon, whereas making ethylene from two CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ molecules requires twelve electrons and formation of a carbon–carbon bond. Experiments on different metal electrodes find different product distributions even with the same reactant. Hori et al. (1994)

Turning a periodic slab into a half-cell calculation

To compare two candidate reaction paths, we can keep just the working surface and the adjacent reaction region. A periodic supercell repeats a slab of catalyst with a specified coverage of adsorbates. We propose structures for the bound intermediates, relax the atoms, and calculate their Kohn–Sham energies. Explicit water or an electrolyte model can change the relative energies of exposed, charged or hydrogen-bonded groups. Gas molecules, dissolved species, electrons and protons each need a consistent reference.

For an intermediate iii, a typical free-energy estimate is

Gi(T)≃Ei,DFT+Ei,ZP+ΔHi,thermal(T)−TSi(T)+ΔGi,solv.G_i(T)\simeq E_{i,\mathrm{DFT}}+E_{i,\mathrm{ZP}} +\Delta H_{i,\mathrm{thermal}}(T)-TS_i(T)+\Delta G_{i,\mathrm{solv}} . Gi​(T)≃Ei,DFT​+Ei,ZP​+ΔHi,thermal​(T)−TSi​(T)+ΔGi,solv​.

The harmonic zero-point energy is Ei,ZP=12∑jhνijE_{i,\mathrm{ZP}}=\tfrac12\sum_j h\nu_{ij}Ei,ZP​=21​∑j​hνij​ and remains finite at zero temperature. In contrast, the vibrational thermal excitation energy is ∑jhνij/[exp⁡(hνij/kBT)−1]\sum_j h\nu_{ij}/[\exp(h\nu_{ij}/k_{\mathrm B}T)-1]∑j​hνij​/[exp(hνij​/kB​T)−1] and vanishes there. If the DFT model already includes solvation, only missing solvent contributions belong in the last term. Gas-phase entropy can be substantial when comparing a free molecule with one confined to a surface site.

The computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) supplies the chemical potential of a proton–electron pair without calculating an isolated solvated proton. At standard hydrogen pressure,

μ~H++μ~e=12GH2−eUSHE−kBTln⁡(10) pH.\tilde\mu_{\mathrm H^+}+\tilde\mu_e =\tfrac12 G_{\mathrm H_2}-eU_{\mathrm{SHE}} -k_{\mathrm B}T\ln(10)\,\mathrm{pH}. μ~​H+​+μ~​e​=21​GH2​​−eUSHE​−kB​Tln(10)pH.

At 298 K298\,\mathrm K298K the last term is −0.0592 eV-0.0592\,\mathrm{eV}−0.0592eV per pH unit. A reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) equilibrates hydrogen with the solution at its actual pH. Thus URHE=USHE+(kBTln⁡10/e) pHU_{\mathrm{RHE}}=U_{\mathrm{SHE}}+(k_{\mathrm B}T\ln 10/e)\,\mathrm{pH}URHE​=USHE​+(kB​Tln10/e)pH and the pair chemical potential is simply 12GH2−eURHE\tfrac12 G_{\mathrm H_2}-eU_{\mathrm{RHE}}21​GH2​​−eURHE​. For hydrogenation, A∗+H++e−→AH∗\mathrm A^*+\mathrm H^++e^-\rightarrow\mathrm{AH}^*A∗+H++e−→AH∗, the pair occurs on the reactant side. Its minus sign becomes a plus in the reaction free energy.

ΔG(URHE)=GAH∗−GA∗−12GH2+eURHE.\Delta G(U_{\mathrm{RHE}}) =G_{\mathrm{AH}^*}-G_{\mathrm A^*}-\tfrac12G_{\mathrm H_2} +eU_{\mathrm{RHE}} . ΔG(URHE​)=GAH∗​−GA∗​−21​GH2​​+eURHE​.

For example, a step costing 0.60 eV0.60\,\mathrm{eV}0.60eV at 0 V0\,\mathrm V0V versus RHE costs 0.20 eV0.20\,\mathrm{eV}0.20eV at −0.40 V-0.40\,\mathrm V−0.40V in this approximation. A step consuming two pairs shifts twice as far. Adsorbing a neutral gas molecule without any explicit proton or electron has zero CHE slope if the slab energies themselves are held fixed. Nørskov et al. (2004)

Following six hydrogen additions on gold

Along one associative nitrogen-reduction path, adsorbed nitrogen first gains H to form N2H∗\mathrm{N_2H}^*N2​H∗. The next H goes to the other nitrogen, giving NHNH∗\mathrm{NHNH}^*NHNH∗. The third and fourth additions produce NHNH2∗\mathrm{NHNH_2}^*NHNH2​∗ and NH2NH2∗\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}^*NH2​NH2​∗. A fifth H then allows one NH3\mathrm{NH}_3NH3​ to leave, with NH2∗\mathrm{NH_2}^*NH2​∗ remaining on the surface. The sixth forms the second ammonia molecule and frees the site after desorption. Here ∗^*∗ denotes attachment to the surface. Release of hydrazine from the four-H intermediate would divert the reaction before the two ammonia molecules form.

Bao and co-workers studied tetrahexahedral gold nanorods exposing stepped Au(210) and Au(310) subfacets. They reported ammonia production at ambient temperature and pressure, alongside a smaller hydrazine yield. In their calculated alternating pathway, each horizontal level represents a relaxed intermediate and each vertical difference gives the free energy of the next chemical step. On both facets, binding the initial N2\mathrm N_2N2​ is uphill relative to gas and a clean surface. Hydrogenating it for the first time is substantially more demanding, roughly 1.7 eV1.7\,\mathrm{eV}1.7eV on Au(310) and over 2 eV2\,\mathrm{eV}2eV on Au(210) in the plotted comparison. Au(310) stabilizes the first hydrogenated species more effectively, yet the early uphill step remains large. Bao et al. (2017)

A step's free-energy change compares two minima. Its activation free energy ΔG‡=GTS−Ginitial\Delta G^\ddagger=G_{\mathrm{TS}}-G_{\mathrm{initial}}ΔG‡=GTS​−Ginitial​ requires a transition state on the path between them. Connecting horizontal levels with lines supplies no transition-state energy. For a series of one-electron reductions with CHE slopes +e+e+e, the most uphill step at zero potential determines the limiting potential, UL=−max⁡iΔGi(0)/eU_{\mathrm L}=-\max_i\Delta G_i(0)/eUL​=−maxi​ΔGi​(0)/e. At or below this potential all the included electron-transfer steps are thermodynamically downhill. A potential-independent adsorption or desorption step must be checked separately. Predicting an actual current requires kinetics, including competing reactions such as hydrogen evolution.

Why a graphene vacancy helps a metal cluster bind nitrogen

Removing two sulfur ligands exposes a metal atom that can anchor the cluster at a graphene vacancy. A carbon atom at the rim and the exposed metal then grip opposite ends of a nitrogen molecule. In this geometry electrons from the metal can enter the nitrogen antibonding orbitals, weakening the bond that must eventually break. Yao and co-workers identified this site in their study of Au–Pt and Au–Pd clusters on graphene. Yao et al. (2020).

From a ligand-protected cluster to a nitrogen adsorption site

The intact Au4Pt2(SR)8\mathrm{Au}_4\mathrm{Pt}_2(\mathrm{SR})_8Au4​Pt2​(SR)8​ cluster is surrounded by eight sulfur-containing ligands. During anchoring, two SR\mathrm{SR}SR ligands at the bottom are removed. The exposed Pt bonds to C atoms at the graphene defect edge, anchoring Au4Pt2(SR)6\mathrm{Au}_4\mathrm{Pt}_2(\mathrm{SR})_6Au4​Pt2​(SR)6​ at a divacancy: a defect formed by two missing adjacent C atoms.

Ligand removal also changes the electronic states available for bonding. The energy gap decreases, and singly occupied states derived from Pt 5d5d5d and Au 6s6s6s appear. Each contains one electron and lies at relatively high energy, making electron donation to nitrogen easier. The same cluster on defect-free graphene still cannot adsorb N2\mathrm N_2N2​, showing that ligand removal and the defect site must act together.

Adsorbed nitrogen bridges the cluster and the defect C atom. One end forms a C–N bond, while the other forms a metal–N bond with nearby Pt/Au. This two-ended geometry both holds the molecule in place and brings it into contact with C and metal orbitals that can participate in bonding. The proposed local Pt coordination was also assessed by comparing the main peak positions and shapes of simulated and experimental XANES spectra.

The defect C atom and nearby metal bind opposite ends of nitrogen. Charge-density-difference isosurfaces show electron accumulation and depletion after adsorption; blue atoms mark the nitrogen molecule. The XANES comparison tests the model of local Pt coordination.

Donation, back-donation, and weakening of the N–N bond

After adsorption, nitrogen orbitals mix with metal ddd orbitals. Electron transfer occurs in both directions: occupied nitrogen σ\sigmaσ orbitals donate to the metal, and the metal back-donates into nitrogen π∗\pi^*π∗ orbitals. Back-donation increases antibonding occupation and weakens the N–N bond. The system's Fermi level and nitrogen LUMO differ by approximately 0.6 eV0.6\,\mathrm{eV}0.6eV; Bader analysis gives a net gain of about 1.441.441.44 electrons by nitrogen.

The charge-density difference shows where electrons accumulate or are depleted after adsorption:

Δρ(r)=ρcat+N2(r)−ρcat(r)−ρN2(r).\Delta\rho(\mathbf r) =\rho_{\mathrm{cat}+\mathrm N_2}(\mathbf r) -\rho_{\mathrm{cat}}(\mathbf r) -\rho_{\mathrm N_2}(\mathbf r). Δρ(r)=ρcat+N2​​(r)−ρcat​(r)−ρN2​​(r).

All three densities use the same atomic positions as in the adsorbed geometry. Δρ>0\Delta\rho>0Δρ>0 indicates electron accumulation, and Δρ<0\Delta\rho<0Δρ<0 indicates depletion. Integration over selected regions or charge partitioning can further estimate transferred electron numbers. This comparison describes electronic rearrangement in the system containing adsorbed nitrogen.

The adsorption energy is defined as

Eads=Ecat+N2−Ecat−EN2.E_{\mathrm{ads}} =E_{\mathrm{cat}+\mathrm N_2}-E_{\mathrm{cat}}-E_{\mathrm N_2}. Eads​=Ecat+N2​​−Ecat​−EN2​​.

Here, Eads=−0.38 eVE_{\mathrm{ads}}=-0.38\,\mathrm{eV}Eads​=−0.38eV, so adsorption lowers the energy. Activation does not immediately remove the N–N bond: its occupation and bond strength change first, and successive hydrogenation then converts the two N atoms into ammonia.

Successive hydrogenation, desorption, and energy barriers

This pathway first hydrogenates the N atom attached to graphene. Three H atoms are added successively, and the first ammonia molecule is released. Another three H atoms are then added to the N still attached to the metal, releasing the second ammonia molecule. Product desorption frees the site for another catalytic cycle. The final ammonia desorption requires about 0.91 eV0.91\,\mathrm{eV}0.91eV, the largest energy cost along this pathway.

The horizontal axis orders the reaction steps, and the vertical axis gives relative energy. The atomic structures show two successive sequences of hydrogenation and ammonia desorption. Values beside the plateaus are energy changes between consecutive steps; intermediate-state energies and transition-state barriers are different quantities.

The heights of these plateaus refer to intermediates. Each added H also brings a proton and an electron from the reservoirs. Comparing plateaus therefore requires a common hydrogen reference; locating a kinetic barrier would require the transition state between them.

Production rate and Faradaic efficiency

The experimental rates are reported per unit catalyst mass and time, at potentials relative to RHE. At −0.1 V-0.1\,\mathrm V−0.1V, graphene-supported Pt clusters produce ammonia at approximately three times the rate of unsupported clusters; the Pd system reaches its peak at −0.2 V-0.2\,\mathrm V−0.2V.

More negative potentials also promote the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). The Pd system suppresses HER more effectively, allowing a higher ammonia production rate at a more negative potential. Optimizing the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) therefore requires both promoting nitrogen activation and hydrogenation and reducing the fraction of electrons consumed by hydrogen evolution.

Faradaic efficiency measures the fraction of total charge used to produce ammonia:

FENH3=3FnNH3Q.\mathrm{FE}_{\mathrm{NH}_3} =\frac{3F n_{\mathrm{NH}_3}}{Q}. FENH3​​=Q3FnNH3​​​.

FFF is the Faraday constant, nNH3n_{\mathrm{NH}_3}nNH3​​ is the amount of ammonia produced in moles, and QQQ is the total charge passed. The factor 3 follows from the three electrons required per ammonia molecule. Production rate describes how quickly ammonia is made; FE describes how efficiently electrons are used for that purpose. If the current doubles while the ammonia production rate stays fixed, QQQ doubles over the same time interval and FE halves.

Modelling an electrode held at constant potential

Which part of the cell can exchange electrons?

When nitrogen binds to gold, it redistributes charge and changes the surface dipole. In a calculation at fixed excess charge, the electrode potential can shift as a consequence. At an experimental electrode connected to a potentiostat, electrons can instead flow through the circuit until the electrode returns to the set potential. The two procedures compare different final states even if they start from the same clean surface.

A constant-charge calculation (DFT-CC) specifies the electron number for each supercell composition. Charge can still move internally between the slab and an adsorbate. Fixed electron number alone does not imply that the system is isolated: an isolated system fixes N,V,EN,V,EN,V,E, while a system in contact with a heat bath can fix N,V,TN,V,TN,V,T. A constant-potential calculation (DFT-CP) treats the electrode as an open subsystem in local electronic equilibrium with a reservoir at μ~e\tilde\mu_eμ~​e​. Overall charge is conserved as the reservoir supplies electrons and the electrolyte provides compensating charge.

For atomic geometry R\mathbf RR and fixed temperature and volume, the electronic grand potential can be written

Ω(R,μ~e)=min⁡Ne[F(R,Ne)−μ~eNe].\Omega(\mathbf R,\tilde\mu_e)= \min_{N_e}\left[F(\mathbf R,N_e)-\tilde\mu_e N_e\right]. Ω(R,μ~​e​)=Ne​min​[F(R,Ne​)−μ~​e​Ne​].

Here FFF is the Helmholtz free energy at constrained mean electron number NeN_eNe​. At a smooth minimum, ∂F/∂Ne=μ~e\partial F/\partial N_e=\tilde\mu_e∂F/∂Ne​=μ~​e​. The clean surface and the adsorbed surface may therefore have different equilibrium electron numbers at the same potential. Comparing their grand potentials accounts for the work of transferring these electrons. A periodic implementation also needs a potential reference and a treatment of the countercharge. Lozovoi and colleagues developed an early charged-slab scheme that specified the electron chemical potential relative to a reference plane at finite distance. Lozovoi et al. (2001)

Two hypothetical geometries have different charging energies. At fixed charge (left), compare the two dots at Q=0Q=0Q=0 and A lies lower. At fixed potential (right), minimize F−UQF-UQF−UQ on each curve. At U=−0.50 VU=-0.50\,\mathrm VU=−0.50V, B draws more electrons from the circuit and becomes the lower-energy geometry. Negative QQQ means the electrode has gained electrons.

Why a neutral adsorbate can respond to voltage

Suppose the surface charge QiQ_iQi​ in state iii varies locally as Qi=Ci(U−Ui0)Q_i=C_i(U-U_i^0)Qi​=Ci​(U−Ui0​), where CiC_iCi​ is its differential capacitance and Ui0U_i^0Ui0​ its potential of zero charge. At fixed composition, the charging contribution to the fixed-potential free energy satisfies dΩich/dU=−Qid\Omega_i^{\mathrm{ch}}/dU=-Q_idΩich​/dU=−Qi​. Integrating gives

Ωich(U)−Ωich(Ui0)=−12Ci(U−Ui0)2.\Omega_i^{\mathrm{ch}}(U)-\Omega_i^{\mathrm{ch}}(U_i^0) =-\tfrac12 C_i(U-U_i^0)^2 . Ωich​(U)−Ωich​(Ui0​)=−21​Ci​(U−Ui0​)2.

A plot against UUU is a downward-opening parabola over the range of nearly constant capacitance. The minus sign includes the work done by the voltage source. For adsorption we subtract the curve for the clean electrode from that for the covered electrode. An adsorbate that shifts the potential of zero charge can produce a linear voltage dependence even when the two capacitances agree. Different capacitances add curvature. Both effects can occur with zero formal electron transfer in the balanced adsorption reaction.

One example involves a cobalt atom coordinated by four nitrogen atoms in carbon. Different occupations of its ddd orbitals give different spin states. Binding an oxygen reduction intermediate can change both the spin and the orientation of the adsorbate. Duan and Henkelman calculated separate fixed-potential energy curves for these states. For bound hydroperoxyl, OOH∗\mathrm{OOH}^*OOH∗, changes in dipole and charging shifted their relative stability. Allowing the most stable spin state to change raised the predicted acidic oxygen-reduction onset potential from 0.540.540.54 to 0.80 V0.80\,\mathrm V0.80V versus RHE compared with keeping the hydroperoxyl complex in its low-spin state. A spin state chosen from the neutral structure alone would thus give a different answer to a chemical question. Duan and Henkelman (2020)

Charging an electrode and passing a steady current

For N2\mathrm N_2N2​ on Au(310), one can compare an end-on configuration, where one nitrogen meets the metal, with a side-on configuration, where both do. In a fixed-charge CHE calculation, each neutral adsorption energy is a horizontal line against potential. Each corresponding singly hydrogenated state has acquired one proton–electron pair, so its relative formation energy rises by 1 eV1\,\mathrm{eV}1eV for a 1 V1\,\mathrm V1V increase in potential. The intercepts contain the different binding geometries. The common slope follows from the assumed electron count.

In a comparison by Wang and co-workers, fixed-potential DFT gave weak curvature for side-on nitrogen adsorption. Its adsorption free energy remained positive over the potential interval studied. At −0.85 V-0.85\,\mathrm V−0.85V versus RHE the first hydrogenation cost 0.74 eV0.74\,\mathrm{eV}0.74eV at fixed charge and 0.78 eV0.78\,\mathrm{eV}0.78eV at fixed potential. Both models therefore identified the same costly step on this surface, despite treating electrode charging differently. Wang et al. (2025 preprint), Figs. 2–3

At fixed potential a half-cell calculation equilibrates the instantaneous electronic structure with one reservoir. A current-carrying cell can maintain different electron electrochemical potentials at its two electrodes, and oxidation and reduction continuously replenish the carriers passing through the circuit. Local equilibrium at a metal surface may still be a good approximation when electrons relax rapidly between rare transfer events. To ask whether a sustained current itself changes bond occupations or forces, one must specify how carriers enter and leave the reaction region. That requires an electronic transport model in addition to a choice between fixed charge and fixed potential.

Coherent conduction in an open junction

When a relaxation time stops describing the device

In a long, uniform wire, it makes sense to ask how much current a local electric field produces. Suppose electrons occupy a nearly parabolic band, with carrier density nnn, effective mass m∗m^*m∗ and momentum relaxation time τ\tauτ. A field E\mathcal EE accelerates a carrier of charge −e-e−e, where e>0e>0e>0, while scattering relaxes its average drift velocity. The steady balance gives

0=−eE−m∗vdτ,j=−nevd=σE,σ=ne2τm∗.0=-e\mathcal E-\frac{m^*v_{\rm d}}{\tau}, \qquad j=-ne v_{\rm d}=\sigma\mathcal E, \qquad \sigma=\frac{ne^2\tau}{m^*}. 0=−eE−τm∗vd​​,j=−nevd​=σE,σ=m∗ne2τ​.

The band curvature sets the mass: in one dimension, 1/m∗=ℏ−2d2E/dk21/m^*=\hbar^{-2}d^2E/dk^21/m∗=ℏ−2d2E/dk2. The periodic ionic potential is already part of the band structure; phonons and disorder are examples of what relaxes momentum. This Drude description is useful when a carrier scatters many times over the length of the wire.

A short contact can be quite different. When its length is comparable to or smaller than the mean free path, an electron can cross without a momentum-relaxing collision. If the length is also shorter than the phase-coherence length, amplitudes reflected at different sites can interfere. Ballistic and coherent describe different conditions: elastic reflection can preserve phase even though it reverses momentum. An effective mass may still be useful for computing waves near a band edge; what breaks down is the assumption that a local bulk conductivity describes the resistance of the entire contact. The relevant question becomes: what fraction of the electrons incident from one electrode emerges in the other?

Counting incident modes gives the Landauer current

Consider a device connected to two large electrodes, or reservoirs, kept at electrochemical potentials μL\mu_LμL​ and μR\mu_RμR​. Deep inside each electrode the crystal supports propagating Bloch modes. An electron incident from the left in mode nnn scatters into reflected modes of the left lead and transmitted modes of the right. For a simple one-dimensional channel the asymptotic wave has the form

ψ(x)={eikLx+re−ikLx,x in the left lead,teikRx,x in the right lead.\psi(x)= \begin{cases} e^{ik_Lx}+r e^{-ik_Lx}, & x\text{ in the left lead},\\ t e^{ik_Rx}, & x\text{ in the right lead}. \end{cases} ψ(x)={eikL​x+re−ikL​x,teikR​x,​x in the left lead,x in the right lead.​

This is an open boundary condition: the incident amplitude is prescribed, and outgoing waves are free to escape. In a continuum model with constant mass and a finite potential step, matching the wavefunction and its first derivative fixes rrr and ttt. The transmitted probability is a ratio of fluxes, (vR/vL)∣t∣2(v_R/v_L)|t|^2(vR​/vL​)∣t∣2, with vL,vRv_L,v_RvL​,vR​ the positive speeds of the incident and transmitted waves. In a basis normalized to unit incident flux, the velocity factors are already included. The transmission summed over propagating modes is then

T(E)=∑m,n∣tmn(E)∣2=Tr⁡(t†t).\mathcal T(E)=\sum_{m,n}|t_{mn}(E)|^2 =\operatorname{Tr}(t^\dagger t). T(E)=m,n∑​∣tmn​(E)∣2=Tr(t†t).

With elastic scattering, reflection and transmission probabilities for one incident mode sum to one. Each eigenvalue of t†tt^\dagger tt†t lies between zero and one; the total can exceed one when several channels conduct.

Why does a perfectly transmitted channel give the same conductance whatever its velocity? Normalize a single right-moving lead mode of one spin in a length LLL. In an interval dkdkdk there are L dk/(2π)L\,dk/(2\pi)Ldk/(2π) states, and each crosses a fixed section at rate v/Lv/Lv/L. Since v=ℏ−1dE/dkv=\hbar^{-1}dE/dkv=ℏ−1dE/dk, their product is

L2πdkdE dE  vL=dEh.\frac{L}{2\pi}\frac{dk}{dE}\,dE\;\frac{v}{L} =\frac{dE}{h}. 2πL​dEdk​dELv​=hdE​.

Slow carriers cross less often, but there are proportionally more states in the same energy interval. Multiply this incident rate by the occupation and transmission, then subtract the flux incident from the other reservoir. With fα(E)=[1+exp⁡((E−μα)/(kBT))]−1f_\alpha(E)=[1+\exp((E-\mu_\alpha)/(k_{\rm B}T))]^{-1}fα​(E)=[1+exp((E−μα​)/(kB​T))]−1 and V=(μL−μR)/eV=(\mu_L-\mu_R)/eV=(μL​−μR​)/e, the usual two-terminal current convention gives

I(V)=2eh∫−∞∞T(E,V)[fL(E)−fR(E)] dE.I(V)=\frac{2e}{h}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathcal T(E,V)[f_L(E)-f_R(E)]\,dE. I(V)=h2e​∫−∞∞​T(E,V)[fL​(E)−fR​(E)]dE.

The prefactor 2 counts two equivalent spins. For spin-dependent transport, replace 2T2\mathcal T2T by the sum of transmissions over spins; a trace over a full spin basis already includes them. At zero temperature and infinitesimal bias the conductance is G0T(EF)G_0\mathcal T(E_F)G0​T(EF​), where G0=2e2/h≃77.5 μSG_0=2e^2/h\simeq77.5\,\mu\mathrm SG0​=2e2/h≃77.5μS. Thus even a perfectly transmitting single channel has a finite two-terminal resistance, 1/G01/G_01/G0​, without momentum loss inside the channel. Landauer related conduction to scattering; Fisher and Lee connected the multichannel transmission matrix to conductance.

What a molecular switch, diode or transistor changes

A molecular bridge admits a simple first interpretation: an incoming Bloch wave couples to a molecular orbital, and that orbital couples to an outgoing wave. Both the orbital energy and the overlap at each contact matter. An orbital close to EFE_FEF​ can carry little current if its symmetry prevents it from coupling to one electrode. In a calculation for nickelocene between two capped carbon nanotubes, Tang and co-workers found that rotating the electrodes relative to each other changed transmission through the spin-polarized frontier orbitals. The molecular energy levels alone would miss the effect.

A switch has two selectable configurations with different conductances at the same readout bias. Quek and co-workers repeatedly stretched and compressed a gold–bipyridine–gold junction. The angle of the nitrogen–gold contact changed how well the electrode coupled to the conducting π\piπ system, giving two conductance states. Light can change the molecule itself: Zhang and co-workers predicted different transmissions for the cis and trans forms of an azobenzene junction. Diarylethene uses a different chemical motion. Ultraviolet light closes a ring and extends conjugation; visible light reopens it. Cai and co-workers calculated the resulting conductance contrast with graphene nanoribbon electrodes. Jia and co-workers observed reversible photoswitching in diarylethene junctions covalently connected to graphene.

A diode is tested at opposite bias polarities with the same configuration. A conventional ppp–nnn junction has a depletion region whose potential barrier responds to the applied voltage. The Aviram–Ratner proposal instead connects donor and acceptor groups through a molecular tunnelling barrier. Bias of one polarity can align orbitals that are far apart in energy at the opposite polarity. To obtain rectification, however, ∣I(V)∣|I(V)|∣I(V)∣ and ∣I(−V)∣|I(-V)|∣I(−V)∣ must actually differ. Unequal fixed contact couplings alone do not ensure this: if T(E)\mathcal T(E)T(E) is unchanged and the reservoir potentials simply exchange, the current reverses sign with the same magnitude. Stokbro, Taylor and Brandbyge calculated donor–acceptor level alignment near 3.8 V3.8\,\mathrm V3.8V in one gold-contacted molecule, yet found poor rectification because appreciable current also flowed in reverse.

A field-effect transistor has a third electrode. The gate shifts levels relative to the source and drain; the source–drain bias drives the measured current. The current falls when the gate shifts the frontier-orbital resonances far enough that the bias window lies in the gap between them. Tunnelling tails generally leave some leakage. Meng and co-workers combined an electrostatic gate with optical control in a ruthenium–diarylethene junction, allowing the current to be changed either by shifting the level alignment or by changing the molecular structure.

Conducting channels in wires, ribbons and sheets

The most literal demonstration of channel counting is a wire pulled down to one atomic row. Ohnishi, Kondo and Takayanagi imaged a suspended gold contact while measuring its conductance. As the neck narrowed, a contact with two atomic strands carried about 2G02G_02G0​, and a single strand about G0G_0G0​ before it broke. These plateaus reflect nearly open channels in that contact; counting atoms is not a general replacement for calculating transmission.

In a carbon nanotube, motion around the circumference is quantized while carriers propagate along the axis. A semiconducting nanotube can therefore serve as a one-dimensional transistor channel between metal contacts, as Tans, Verschueren and Dekker demonstrated at room temperature. Arrays provide several tubes in parallel. A transfer curve sweeps the gate voltage at fixed drain bias to show how effectively the channel turns off; an output curve sweeps the drain bias at fixed gate voltage. A graphene nanoribbon confines motion across its width instead; its width and edges select the allowed subbands. Llinas and co-workers measured gate-dependent current in armchair ribbons only nine or thirteen carbon atoms wide.

A two-dimensional channel retains a continuum of in-plane propagation directions. Monolayer MoS2\mathrm{MoS_2}MoS2​ has a direct band gap at KKK, so a gate can move a band edge past the source Fermi level and turn the channel on. Mak and co-workers identified the change to a direct gap in the monolayer. The interface can matter as much as the channel: Ma and co-workers compared MoS2\mathrm{MoS_2}MoS2​ transistors with and without hexagonal boron nitride between the channel and SiO2\mathrm{SiO_2}SiO2​. The measured room-temperature mobilities were about 909090 and 56 cm2 V−1 s−156\,\mathrm{cm^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}56cm2V−1s−1, respectively.

Free-standing graphene lacks an intrinsic gap. Zhou and co-workers reported a gap near the Dirac point in epitaxial graphene on silicon carbide that diminished as more graphene layers were added. In a distinct material, the ordered carbon buffer layer partly bonded to SiC, Zhao and co-workers reported a gap of about 0.6 eV0.6\,\mathrm{eV}0.6eV. A substrate can thus change the channel's electronic spectrum itself, as distinct from changing the rate at which carriers scatter.

Green's functions and open electrodes

A point source reveals the spectrum

Direct wave matching works for a potential step; an atomistic junction has many electrode modes at every energy. A Green's function collects the response to any incident source. Introduce a complex energy zzz and consider a driven equation (zI−H)∣ψ⟩=∣s⟩(zI-H)|\psi\rangle=|s\rangle(zI−H)∣ψ⟩=∣s⟩. Its solution is ∣ψ⟩=G(z)∣s⟩|\psi\rangle=G(z)|s\rangle∣ψ⟩=G(z)∣s⟩, where

(zI−H)G(z)=I,G(z)=(zI−H)−1.(zI-H)G(z)=I, \qquad G(z)=(zI-H)^{-1}. (zI−H)G(z)=I,G(z)=(zI−H)−1.

The hat in G^\hat GG^ denotes the operator. Choosing orbitals ∣i⟩|i\rangle∣i⟩ and ∣j⟩|j\rangle∣j⟩ gives an ordinary matrix element Gij=⟨i∣G^∣j⟩G_{ij}=\langle i|\hat G|j\rangleGij​=⟨i∣G^∣j⟩. In position space the identity on the right is δ(r−r′)\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')δ(r−r′). Thus G(r,r′;z)G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r';z)G(r,r′;z) is the amplitude response at r\mathbf rr to a unit source at r′\mathbf r'r′. To select outgoing waves and a causal response, approach the real energy axis from above: Gr(E)=[(E+i0+)I−H]−1G^r(E)=[(E+i0^+)I-H]^{-1}Gr(E)=[(E+i0+)I−H]−1. The advanced function approaches from below, Ga=(Gr)†G^a=(G^r)^\daggerGa=(Gr)† on the real axis.

For an isolated Hamiltonian with eigenpairs (En,∣n⟩)(E_n,|n\rangle)(En​,∣n⟩), expanding the inverse in its eigenbasis gives

Gr(E)=∑n∣n⟩⟨n∣E−En+i0+,A(E)=i(Gr−Ga)=2π∑n∣n⟩⟨n∣δ(E−En).G^r(E)=\sum_n\frac{|n\rangle\langle n|}{E-E_n+i0^+}, \qquad A(E)=i(G^r-G^a)=2\pi\sum_n|n\rangle\langle n|\delta(E-E_n). Gr(E)=n∑​E−En​+i0+∣n⟩⟨n∣​,A(E)=i(Gr−Ga)=2πn∑​∣n⟩⟨n∣δ(E−En​).

The poles locate the allowed energies; their weights locate the states in space. The local density of states per spin is A(r,r;E)/(2π)A(\mathbf r,\mathbf r;E)/(2\pi)A(r,r;E)/(2π). Multiplying the spectral function by the equilibrium occupation and integrating gives the one-particle density matrix,

ρ=12π∫f(E−μ)A(E) dE=−1πIm⁡∫−∞μGr(E) dE(T=0 in the last expression).\rho=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int f(E-\mu)A(E)\,dE =-\frac{1}{\pi}\operatorname{Im}\int_{-\infty}^{\mu}G^r(E)\,dE \quad(T=0\text{ in the last expression}). ρ=2π1​∫f(E−μ)A(E)dE=−π1​Im∫−∞μ​Gr(E)dE(T=0 in the last expression).

For a matrix, Im⁡M=(M−M†)/(2i)\operatorname{Im}M=(M-M^\dagger)/(2i)ImM=(M−M†)/(2i). The real-space diagonal ρ(r,r)\rho(\mathbf r,\mathbf r)ρ(r,r) gives the electron number density; multiply by −e-e−e for the electronic charge density. The eigenstate expansion explains why the method works. Computing the inverse does not require knowing those eigenstates first.

Eliminating a semi-infinite lead

Separate a Hamiltonian as H=H0+UH=H_0+UH=H0​+U, where the scattering potential or contact coupling UUU is added to a problem with known propagator g=(zI−H0)−1g=(zI-H_0)^{-1}g=(zI−H0​)−1. The inverse identity gives the Dyson equation G=g+gUGG=g+gUGG=g+gUG, equivalently G=g+GUgG=g+GUgG=g+GUg. Iterating produces g+gUg+gUgUg+⋯g+gUg+gUgUg+\cdotsg+gUg+gUgUg+⋯: between successive scattering events the electron propagates with ggg.

Now take H0H_0H0​ to contain separate left, device and right blocks. Let HDα=HαD†H_{D\alpha}=H_{\alpha D}^\daggerHDα​=HαD†​ couple the device to lead α\alphaα. The lead row of (zI−H)G=I(zI-H)G=I(zI−H)G=I gives GαD=gαHαDGDDG_{\alpha D}=g_\alpha H_{\alpha D}G_{DD}GαD​=gα​HαD​GDD​. GDr(E)=[(E+i0+)I−HD−ΣLr(E)−ΣRr(E)]−1,Σαr=HDαgαrHαD.G_D^r(E)=\left[(E+i0^+)I-H_D-\Sigma_L^r(E)-\Sigma_R^r(E)\right]^{-1}, \qquad \Sigma_\alpha^r=H_{D\alpha}g_\alpha^r H_{\alpha D}. GDr​(E)=[(E+i0+)I−HD​−ΣLr​(E)−ΣRr​(E)]−1,Σαr​=HDα​gαr​HαD​.

Only lead sites attached to the device enter this product, so only the surface Green's function of each semi-infinite electrode is needed. Read the product from right to left: an amplitude leaves the device, propagates in the lead, and returns to the device. Some probability escapes to infinity. Its real energy shift is encoded by the Hermitian part of Σr\Sigma^rΣr; its escape width is

Γα=i(Σαr−Σαa)=−2Im⁡Σαr.\Gamma_\alpha=i(\Sigma_\alpha^r-\Sigma_\alpha^a) =-2\operatorname{Im}\Sigma_\alpha^r. Γα​=i(Σαr​−Σαa​)=−2ImΣαr​.
