Gr=1E−ϵ~0+iΓ/2,A(E)=Γ(E−ϵ~0)2+(Γ/2)2.G^r=\frac{1}{E-\tilde\epsilon_0+i\Gamma/2}, \qquad A(E)=\frac{\Gamma}{(E-\tilde\epsilon_0)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}. Gr=E−ϵ~0​+iΓ/21​,A(E)=(E−ϵ~0​)2+(Γ/2)2Γ​.

Its full width at half maximum is Γ\GammaΓ, in energy units. Stronger coupling shortens the time an electron remains on the level and broadens its spectral peak.

In a Kohn–Sham calculation the device block includes the molecule and several electrode layers. These layers allow contact charge transfer and screening to develop before the calculation is matched to bulk electrode densities and potentials. An equilibrium calculation updates HD[ρ]H_D[\rho]HD​[ρ], GDrG_D^rGDr​ and ρ\rhoρ until the density stops changing. In a localized nonorthogonal basis with overlap matrix SSS, the matrix to partition is zS−HzS-HzS−H; both the device block and the couplings must use that convention. A useful boundary check comes from the C60\mathrm{C}_{60}C60​ junction studied by Taylor, Guo and Wang: their equilibrium charge-density contours join smoothly across the artificial boundaries inside the aluminium leads. The molecule itself need not resemble its isolated state. Charge transfer brought its lowest unoccupied orbital into alignment with the electrode Fermi level; the calculated conductance was about 2.2G02.2G_02.2G0​, requiring more than one transmitting channel.

Occupation and current at finite bias

Which electrode fills a device state?

A convenient bias convention is μL=μ+eV/2\mu_L=\mu+eV/2μL​=μ+eV/2 and μR=μ−eV/2\mu_R=\mu-eV/2μR​=μ−eV/2. This choice fixes the difference between reservoirs; the voltage need not drop symmetrically within the device. The two reservoirs do not generally establish a single Fermi distribution inside it. A resonance in the interval μR<E<μL\mu_R<E<\mu_LμR​<E<μL​ at zero temperature has occupied incident states on the left and empty ones on the right. Its spectrum tells us that an electron can occupy the state, not how strongly it is populated. The lesser Green's function supplies the missing information:

Gij<(t,t′)=i⟨cj†(t′)ci(t)⟩,ρij=−iGij<(t,t)=−i2π∫Gij<(E) dE.G^<_{ij}(t,t')=i\langle c_j^\dagger(t')c_i(t)\rangle, \qquad \rho_{ij}=-iG^<_{ij}(t,t) =-\frac{i}{2\pi}\int G^<_{ij}(E)\,dE. Gij<​(t,t′)=i⟨cj†​(t′)ci​(t)⟩,ρij​=−iGij<​(t,t)=−2πi​∫Gij<​(E)dE.

The superscript <<< labels this particular ordering of creation and annihilation operators. Taking t=t′t=t't=t′ returns an occupation, whereas GrG^rGr gives the response to the source. Here cic_ici​ annihilates an electron on orbital iii. A steady state is invariant under a common shift of both times, so Fourier transformation in t−t′t-t't−t′ gives one energy argument. The last equality uses that energy representation. For independent thermal reservoirs and coherent effective single-particle motion in the device, the occupied incident states enter through

Σ<=i(ΓLfL+ΓRfR),G<=GrΣ<Ga.\Sigma^<=i(\Gamma_L f_L+\Gamma_R f_R), \qquad G^<=G^r\Sigma^<G^a. Σ<=i(ΓL​fL​+ΓR​fR​),G<=GrΣ<Ga.

The reservoir supplies the occupation; GrG^rGr propagates each injected amplitude, and GaG^aGa propagates its conjugate. Their product forms a density matrix. With Aα=GrΓαGaA_\alpha=G^r\Gamma_\alpha G^aAα​=GrΓα​Ga, the device density is therefore

ρ=12π∫(ALfL+ARfR) dE.\rho=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int (A_L f_L+A_R f_R)\,dE. ρ=2π1​∫(AL​fL​+AR​fR​)dE.

This lead-injection formula counts states connected to at least one reservoir. A true bound state decoupled from both would require a separate occupation. Each conducting orbital can receive contributions from both reservoirs. For the single resonance above, Aα=AΓα/ΓA_\alpha=A\Gamma_\alpha/\GammaAα​=AΓα​/Γ. Within the zero-temperature bias window, the occupied fraction of its spectral weight is ΓL/Γ\Gamma_L/\GammaΓL​/Γ, which equals one half for symmetric contacts. If instead ΓL=4ΓR\Gamma_L=4\Gamma_RΓL​=4ΓR​, it is four fifths: the left electrode fills the state more readily than the right empties it. This is an energy-resolved fraction; the total level occupation still requires integrating the resonance, including its tails.

Common occupation, the bias window and numerical integration

For states coupled to the leads, the inverse identity Gr−Ga=Gr[(Ga)−1−(Gr)−1]GaG^r-G^a=G^r[(G^a)^{-1}-(G^r)^{-1}]G^aGr−Ga=Gr[(Ga)−1−(Gr)−1]Ga gives A=AL+ARA=A_L+A_RA=AL​+AR​. Add and subtract ALfRA_L f_RAL​fR​ in the density:

ρ=12π∫AfR dE+12π∫AL(fL−fR) dE.\rho=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int A f_R\,dE+ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int A_L(f_L-f_R)\,dE. ρ=2π1​∫AfR​dE+2π1​∫AL​(fL​−fR​)dE.

The first term fills all available states using the right reservoir as reference. It uses the Hamiltonian at the actual bias, not a separate zero-voltage calculation. The second corrects the occupation of states incident from the left. At zero temperature and μL>μR\mu_L>\mu_RμL​>μR​, the result is

ρ=−1πIm⁡∫−∞μRGr(E) dE+12π∫μRμLGrΓLGa dE.\rho=-\frac{1}{\pi}\operatorname{Im}\int_{-\infty}^{\mu_R}G^r(E)\,dE +\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mu_R}^{\mu_L}G^r\Gamma_LG^a\,dE. ρ=−π1​Im∫−∞μR​​Gr(E)dE+2π1​∫μR​μL​​GrΓL​GadE.

This split saves work. The first integral extends deep into the occupied bands, where sharp real-axis peaks would demand fine sampling. A retarded propagator is analytic above the real energy axis, so its path between fixed endpoints can be deformed upwards into the complex plane, away from the peaks. The second integral contains both GrG^rGr and GaG^aGa, with singularities on opposite sides; it is usually evaluated on the real axis over the relatively narrow bias window. At finite temperature the Fermi edges broaden, and the general all-energy expression with fL−fRf_L-f_RfL​−fR​ is needed. A contour integration that includes a finite-temperature Fermi function must also account for its poles.

How much of the occupied spectrum transmits?

To compute a current one needs propagation between the contacts. For elastic transport, the transmission can be evaluated without constructing scattering wavefunctions channel by channel:

T(E,V)=Tr⁡[ΓLGrΓRGa].\mathcal T(E,V)=\operatorname{Tr} \big[\Gamma_L G^r\Gamma_R G^a\big]. T(E,V)=Tr[ΓL​GrΓR​Ga].

This is the Caroli expression. A level coupled to only one electrode can contribute to the density while carrying no through-current: one of the two coupling factors in the transmission vanishes. For the single resonance with constant widths the result is

T(E)=ΓLΓR(E−ϵ~0)2+(Γ/2)2,T(ϵ~0)=4ΓLΓR(ΓL+ΓR)2.\mathcal T(E)=\frac{\Gamma_L\Gamma_R}{(E-\tilde\epsilon_0)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}, \qquad \mathcal T(\tilde\epsilon_0)=\frac{4\Gamma_L\Gamma_R}{(\Gamma_L+\Gamma_R)^2}. T(E)=(E−ϵ~0​)2+(Γ/2)2ΓL​ΓR​​,T(ϵ~0​)=(ΓL​+ΓR​)24ΓL​ΓR​​.

Matched contacts give unit transmission on resonance, even for a very narrow peak. With the same four-to-one imbalance as above, the peak transmission falls to 16/25=0.6416/25=0.6416/25=0.64: the more heavily occupied resonance is the less effective bridge. If this level sits at EFE_FEF​ and is spin degenerate, its zero-temperature linear conductance is 0.64G00.64G_00.64G0​, about 49.6 μS49.6\,\mu\mathrm S49.6μS. At finite bias it is the area under the transmission within the occupied incident energy range that matters, not just the peak height.

Both junctions have the same level energy and total linewidth, ΓL+ΓR=0.10 eV\Gamma_L+\Gamma_R=0.10\,\mathrm{eV}ΓL​+ΓR​=0.10eV, so their local densities of states coincide in the upper panel. Redistributing that width between the contacts lowers the transmission peak from 111 to 0.640.640.64. At zero temperature only the area under each transmission curve inside the shaded bias window contributes to the current.

In a self-consistent device calculation, set the two reservoir potentials, update the biased Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian and lead self-energies, calculate GrG^rGr and G<G^<G<, and return the resulting charge density to the potential calculation. Once the density and potential converge, insert the resulting T(E,V)\mathcal T(E,V)T(E,V) into the Landauer current. At equal temperature and chemical potential, the current vanishes even if the junction has a large density of states and transmits perfectly: right-going and left-going fluxes cancel. Applying bias upsets that cancellation and can also change the spectrum through the charge it redistributes.

Electronic structure in a current-carrying steady state

Imagine loading one more right-moving state in a wire and emptying a left-moving state of the same energy. If the two have equal probability density, the wire's charge density stays the same, but its current changes. This is the missing information when one tries to describe a biased junction by its equilibrium ground-state density alone. In an ordinary time-reversal-symmetric conductor at equilibrium, states of opposite velocity have equal occupations and their currents cancel. Under bias, a state incident from the left reservoir and one incident from the right can have different occupations at the same energy. Inside a molecule, reflection mixes directions of motion; the useful label is the reservoir of incidence, not the sign of a local momentum.

Conventional DFT combined with nonequilibrium Green's functions (DFT+NEGF) already distinguishes the two reservoirs. It can calculate a nonzero current and update the electrostatic potential under bias. The question for steady-state density functional theory (SS-DFT) is narrower: should the effective electron-electron potential itself depend on how the states are populated? Liu, Nurbawono and Zhang (2015) proposed a two-density theory for this purpose.

Why a driven state can have an equilibrium-like statistical weight

Take two macroscopic reservoirs at the same temperature, with electrochemical potentials μL\mu_LμL​ and μR\mu_RμR​. Set e>0e>0e>0 and eVb=μL−μReV_b=\mu_L-\mu_ReVb​=μL​−μR​. In Hershfield's formulation, a steady-state expectation value can be written as

⟨A^⟩ss=Tr⁡ ⁣[e−β(H^−Y^)A^]Tr⁡ ⁣[e−β(H^−Y^)],β=1kBT.\langle\hat A\rangle_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[e^{-\beta(\hat H-\hat Y)}\hat A\right]} {\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[e^{-\beta(\hat H-\hat Y)}\right]}, \qquad \beta=\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm B}T}. ⟨A^⟩ss​=Tr[e−β(H^−Y^)]Tr[e−β(H^−Y^)A^]​,β=kB​T1​.

The bias operator Y^\hat YY^ retains the preparation of the steady state. In a two-reservoir scattering representation, Y^=μLN^L+μRN^R\hat Y=\mu_L\hat N_L+\mu_R\hat N_RY^=μL​N^L​+μR​N^R​. Here N^L\hat N_LN^L​ counts populated incoming scattering states originating in the left reservoir, including their amplitude in the device; it does not count the electrons instantaneously inside the left metal. The analogous statement holds for N^R\hat N_RN^R​. These are the dressed scattering operators of the coupled junction. Their construction in an interacting problem is the difficult part. The resulting Y^\hat YY^ commutes with H^\hat HH^, so the statistical weight is stationary.

Define N^t=N^L+N^R\hat N_t=\hat N_L+\hat N_RN^t​=N^L​+N^R​, N^n=N^L−N^R\hat N_n=\hat N_L-\hat N_RN^n​=N^L​−N^R​ and μˉ=(μL+μR)/2\bar\mu=(\mu_L+\mu_R)/2μˉ​=(μL​+μR​)/2. Substituting N^L,R=(N^t±N^n)/2\hat N_{L,R}=(\hat N_t\pm\hat N_n)/2N^L,R​=(N^t​±N^n​)/2 gives

Y^=μˉN^t+eVb2N^n,H^−Y^=H~−μˉN^t,H~=H^−eVb2N^n.\hat Y=\bar\mu\hat N_t+\frac{eV_b}{2}\hat N_n, \qquad \hat H-\hat Y=\widetilde H-\bar\mu\hat N_t, \qquad \widetilde H=\hat H-\frac{eV_b}{2}\hat N_n. Y^=μˉ​N^t​+2eVb​​N^n​,H^−Y^=H−μˉ​N^t​,H=H^−2eVb​​N^n​.

The exponent now has the form of a grand-canonical weight for an effective Hamiltonian H~\widetilde HH. The physical junction still carries current. The single μˉ\bar\muμˉ​ in the rewritten expression has not erased the two injection conditions: their difference is now in H~\widetilde HH. At zero bias that extra term vanishes.

Which two densities?

In the scattering description let ρL(r)\rho_L(\mathbf r)ρL​(r) and ρR(r)\rho_R(\mathbf r)ρR​(r) denote the local contributions from occupied left- and right-incident states. Their sum is the total density, ρt=ρL+ρR\rho_t=\rho_L+\rho_Rρt​=ρL​+ρR​; their difference, δρLR=ρL−ρR\delta\rho_{LR}=\rho_L-\rho_RδρLR​=ρL​−ρR​, is the formal local population imbalance associated with N^n\hat N_nN^n​. A density has units of particles per volume; current density is charge per unit area per unit time. Determining a flux also requires velocities or transmission amplitudes.

A related but distinct split is useful in actual calculations. For a coherent one-electron junction, write DL(r,E)D_L(\mathbf r,E)DL​(r,E) and DR(r,E)D_R(\mathbf r,E)DR​(r,E) for the local spectral densities supplied by each reservoir, with the spin convention included in DDD. With fα(E)f_\alpha(E)fα​(E) the corresponding Fermi functions, simple rearrangement gives

ρt(r)=∫[DLfL+DRfR] dE=∫(DL+DR)fR dE⏟ρe(r)+∫DL(fL−fR) dE⏟ρn(r).\begin{aligned} \rho_t(\mathbf r) &=\int [D_L f_L+D_R f_R]\,dE\\ &=\underbrace{\int(D_L+D_R)f_R\,dE}_{\rho_e(\mathbf r)} +\underbrace{\int D_L(f_L-f_R)\,dE}_{\rho_n(\mathbf r)}. \end{aligned} ρt​(r)​=∫[DL​fL​+DR​fR​]dE=ρe​(r)∫(DL​+DR​)fR​dE​​+ρn​(r)∫DL​(fL​−fR​)dE​​.​

For μL≥μR\mu_L\geq\mu_RμL​≥μR​, the second term counts the extra population injected by the source above a common reference occupation. At zero temperature only μR<E<μL\mu_R<E<\mu_LμR​<E<μL​ contributes: this is the bias window. The first term is often called the equilibrium component, but its spectral densities can already have changed under bias. It is not the density of the unbiased device.

The distinction matters in an asymmetric contact. The formal difference δρLR\delta\rho_{LR}δρLR​ contains a term ∫(DL−DR)fR dE\int(D_L-D_R)f_R\,dE∫(DL​−DR​)fR​dE in addition to the bias-window population. Even levels below both chemical potentials can have unequal left and right amplitudes at an individual atom. The nonnegative ρn\rho_nρn​ used as a working population in the dual mean-field calculation should therefore not be substituted as an exact pointwise identity for the formal imbalance. The spectral rearrangement above uses one common Hamiltonian; giving the two components different self-consistent potentials is the additional modelling step.

Why vary an effective energy?

In the zero-temperature construction, the bias is conjugate to the integrated imbalance just as the external potential is conjugate to the total density. Writing ρnform=δρLR\rho_n^{\mathrm{form}}=\delta\rho_{LR}ρnform​=δρLR​, the effective energy has the form

E~=Ess[ρt,ρnform]−eVb2∫ρnform(r) d3r.\widetilde E=E_{\mathrm{ss}}[\rho_t,\rho_n^{\mathrm{form}}] -\frac{eV_b}{2}\int \rho_n^{\mathrm{form}}(\mathbf r)\,d^3r. E=Ess​[ρt​,ρnform​]−2eVb​​∫ρnform​(r)d3r.

EssE_{\mathrm{ss}}Ess​ is the expectation of the physical Hamiltonian; its external-potential term is ∫vextρt d3r\int v_{\mathrm{ext}}\rho_t\,d^3r∫vext​ρt​d3r. Minimizing EssE_{\mathrm{ss}}Ess​ alone omits the energetic contribution paired with the imposed bias.

The proposed uniqueness argument uses the same trial-state logic as the Hohenberg–Kohn proof. Consider two effective Hamiltonians with the same kinetic energy and interactions but different potentials or biases. Fix the energy gauge, reservoir construction and particle-number sector. Suppose they have distinct, nondegenerate effective ground states but the same two densities. If the external couplings are compared using the same density operators, their difference has the same expectation in both states:

C=∫(vext−vext′)ρt d3r−e(Vb−Vb′)2∫ρnform d3r.C=\int (v_{\mathrm{ext}}-v'_{\mathrm{ext}})\rho_t\,d^3r -\frac{e(V_b-V'_b)}{2}\int\rho_n^{\mathrm{form}}\,d^3r. C=∫(vext​−vext′​)ρt​d3r−2e(Vb​−Vb′​)​∫ρnform​d3r.

Using the primed state as a trial state for the unprimed Hamiltonian gives E~0<E~0′+C\widetilde E_0<\widetilde E'_0+CE0​<E0′​+C. Reversing the comparison gives E~0′<E~0−C\widetilde E'_0<\widetilde E_0-CE0′​<E0​−C. Adding the inequalities is impossible. Within that construction the pair of densities specifies the effective problem up to the energy reference; steady-state observables may then be expressed as functionals of the pair. The comparison presupposes a common definition of the reservoir sectors. The short proof for distinct, nondegenerate effective ground states is not a uniqueness theorem for every driven or time-dependent system.

In the proposed working functional, one varies admissible ρe\rho_eρe​ and ρn\rho_nρn​ with ρt=ρe+ρn\rho_t=\rho_e+\rho_nρt​=ρe​+ρn​. The reservoirs fix the boundary conditions; for the constrained device calculation the trial populations are nonnegative and integrate together to the prescribed electron number. The stationary solution minimizes the effective energy over the admissible states. At finite temperature an equilibrium-like variational formulation uses a grand potential including entropy; the energy-only argument above takes the zero-temperature limit.

Two coupled mean fields

The dual mean-field approach of Liu, Feng and Zhang assigns auxiliary orbitals to the common occupied population and to the excess injected population. In the working model the bias term is En=−(eVb/2)∫Dρn(r) d3rE_n=-(eV_b/2)\int_D\rho_n(\mathbf r)\,d^3rEn​=−(eVb​/2)∫D​ρn​(r)d3r, with the excess window population integrated over the device DDD. In the local approximation write the exchange-correlation energy as ∫exc(ρe,ρn) d3r\int e_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho_e,\rho_n)\,d^3r∫exc​(ρe​,ρn​)d3r, where exce_{\mathrm{xc}}exc​ is an energy per volume. The effective-energy formulation varies the two sets of normalized orbitals independently. In atomic units it gives

[−12∇2+vext+vH[ρt]+∂exc∂ρe]ϕie=λieϕie,[−12∇2+vext+vH[ρt]+∂exc∂ρn−eVb2]ϕjn=λjnϕjn.\begin{aligned} \left[-\tfrac12\nabla^2+v_{\mathrm{ext}}+v_H[\rho_t] +\frac{\partial e_{\mathrm{xc}}}{\partial\rho_e}\right]\phi_i^e &=\lambda_i^e\phi_i^e,\\ \left[-\tfrac12\nabla^2+v_{\mathrm{ext}}+v_H[\rho_t] +\frac{\partial e_{\mathrm{xc}}}{\partial\rho_n} -\frac{eV_b}{2}\right]\phi_j^n &=\lambda_j^n\phi_j^n . \end{aligned} [−21​∇2+vext​+vH​[ρt​]+∂ρe​∂exc​​]ϕie​[−21​∇2+vext​+vH​[ρt​]+∂ρn​∂exc​​−2eVb​​]ϕjn​​=λie​ϕie​,=λjn​ϕjn​.​

Both populations feel the Hartree potential of the full charge. Their exchange-correlation potentials differ because varying the window population at fixed ρe\rho_eρe​ is a different operation from varying the background at fixed ρn\rho_nρn​. The explicit −eVb/2-eV_b/2−eVb​/2 comes from differentiating the bias term, not from an extra voltage drop to be added to Poisson's equation. The two equations must be solved together: start with densities, build the potentials, solve with open contacts, reconstruct the densities using the reference and excess occupations, and repeat to consistency. With no bias, the window closes and the equilibrium problem is recovered. The accuracy at finite bias still depends on the chosen two-density exchange-correlation approximation.

The Drude expression σ=ne2τ/m∗\sigma=ne^2\tau/m^*σ=ne2τ/m∗ makes a useful comparison. Band curvature sets the effective mass m∗m^*m∗, but the bulk conductivity also depends on the mobile-carrier density nnn and the momentum relaxation time τ\tauτ. In a short coherent junction, the occupations supplied by the contacts likewise matter alongside the spectrum. The Drude nnn need not vanish at zero bias, whereas the excess window population does. A molecular contact is described by its transmission, not by inserting ρn\rho_nρn​ into the bulk Drude formula.

Why nitrogen and sulfur contacts reverse the Au–Ag conductance order

An amine-terminated silane between gold electrodes conducts better than the corresponding junction with silver electrodes. Replace the amines by thiol linkers and silver conducts better. Neither the bulk conductivity of the metals nor the number of silicon atoms explains that reversal: compare the same linker and backbone length on different metals. For the thiol series, lengthening the chain reduces the conductance roughly exponentially, consistent with tunnelling. Li et al. (2017) measured these trends in single-molecule break junctions.

The nitrogen lone pair forms a donor bond to the metal. For these contacts, the occupied molecular resonance lies closer to the metal Fermi level with Au than with Ag. Sulfur forms a covalent metal–S bond and introduces an interface or gateway state with substantial amplitude on that bond. The Ag–S contact has a distinct resonance about 0.4 eV0.4\,\mathrm{eV}0.4eV below the Fermi level; its Au–S counterpart overlaps the broader occupied molecular resonance. A state need not be spread uniformly along the wire to control how readily electrons enter it. This contact-level alignment was already identified in the experimental authors' transport calculations.

Jiang et al. (2021) tested what changes at finite bias. For the amine-linked junction their conventional DFT+NEGF and SS-DFT calculations gave similar currents, both larger with Au. For the thiol-linked junction, their conventional calculations retained the Au-over-Ag ordering, whereas SS-DFT gave the larger Ag current at biases around and above 0.2 V0.2\,\mathrm V0.2V. The authors called the effect nonequilibrium pulling: a conducting channel concentrated near the source and close to the bias window changes its population as the bias changes. The altered mean field feeds back on transmission within the window. Contact bonding explains why the two linkers are different; the finite-bias comparison tests how sensitive a specific contact model is to that electronic feedback.

When the current changes the molecular geometry

The feedback can also move nuclei. At fixed bias this SS-DFT model assigns atom III a force from the full effective energy:

FI=−∂Ess∂RI+eVb2∂∂RI∫ρn(r) d3r.\mathbf F_I=-\frac{\partial E_{\mathrm{ss}}}{\partial\mathbf R_I} +\frac{eV_b}{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf R_I} \int\rho_n(\mathbf r)\,d^3r . FI​=−∂RI​∂Ess​​+2eVb​​∂RI​∂​∫ρn​(r)d3r.

Moving an atom changes orbital overlap and hence the population injected into the device. Even the first, or regular, force is evaluated with the biased electronic structure. At a stationary geometry the two contributions sum to zero; neither need vanish separately. Using the zero-bias geometry at every voltage is a modelling choice. Other open-system approaches also calculate forces at finite bias.

Wang et al. (2024) simulated a gold-contacted bis(triarylamine) junction from a family of experimentally studied molecular wires. In simulations at 300 K300\,\mathrm K300K with a 2 fs2\,\mathrm{fs}2fs time step, the source contact at 1.4 V1.4\,\mathrm V1.4V rearranged after about 100 fs100\,\mathrm{fs}100fs; the analogous transition did not appear in the 1.3 V1.3\,\mathrm V1.3V trajectory. The average Au–S bond length increased by about 0.3 A˚0.3\,\text{\AA}0.3A˚ while nearby groups rotated. The drop in the bias contribution EnE_nEn​ outweighed the rise in EssE_{\mathrm{ss}}Ess​. The new orientations enhanced coupling between Au 5d5d5d and S 3p3p3p orbitals and introduced transmission peaks inside the bias window. At the same bias, the relaxed contact carried several times the current predicted with the original geometry. The changed force constants offered a separate prediction: five of six selected vibrational modes shifted to higher frequency, with the largest shift in a mode involving the source sulfur and its adjacent phenyl group. These high-bias changes are simulation predictions; the earlier wire experiment investigated conductance under chemical oxidation.

What electrode potential changes in nitrogen reduction

Return to nitrogen on stepped Au(310). A potentiostat sets the working-electrode potential UUU relative to a reference electrode. In the wire calculation, VbV_bVb​ sets the difference between two injecting reservoirs. Translating one into the other requires a model for where the electrons enter and leave the reaction region. When electronic relaxation is fast compared with nuclear motion, one can still relax the atoms on an electronic surface. The choice is which electronic population to use at each geometry.

At −0.85 V-0.85\,\mathrm V−0.85V versus RHE, the fixed-charge and fixed-potential calculations above both found that adding the first H to adsorbed nitrogen costs energy. In a steady-state calculation of the same pathway, this uphill step disappeared. Wang and co-workers traced the change to mixing between Au ddd and nitrogen ppp orbitals. Under bias, occupied states in the transport window acquired more weight on the adsorbate, stabilizing side-on nitrogen and the first hydrogenated intermediate. Wang et al. (2025 preprint), Figs. 2–3

Each of these calculations compares two relaxed intermediates. To predict how fast the first H is added, we would also need the transition state between them. To predict how much ammonia the electrode produces, we would need the surface populations and the competing rate of hydrogen evolution.
